title: Sensor Geometry Challenge
summary: Compare GNSS, gyro, star tracker and ground-station range/bearing. Find what each geometry cannot see.

variants.label: Ground tracking (6-state orbit)
variants.description: Four stations: two range+bearing, two range-only. GNSS available but off.

variants.label: Attitude (12-state rigid body)
variants.description: GNSS, gyro and star tracker on a rotating spacecraft with a thrust arc.

briefing.markdown:
**Two experiments.**

1. **Ground tracking.** No GNSS. Four stations track you as you pass overhead: *Alpha* and *Charlie* give range + azimuth + elevation; *Bravo* and *Delta* give **range only**.
2. **Attitude.** The full 12-state spacecraft. GNSS sees position; the gyro sees body rates; the star tracker (off at first) sees attitude. A thrust arc fires from 200 s to 400 s.

**The tool.** The *Observability* panel stacks $R^{-1/2} H \Phi$ for every measurement planned in a window and reports the **rank**, the condition number and the directions that no measurement can see.

prediction.prompt: In the attitude experiment, with GNSS and the gyro on but the star tracker off, can the filter determine which way the spacecraft points while it is **coasting**?

options.feedback: When not thrusting, attitude has no effect on the orbit, so position measurements can't reveal it.

options.text: No — attitude doesn't affect position until the thruster fires.
options.feedback: Right. During the thrust arc, pitch and yaw tilt the acceleration and become (weakly) observable through GNSS. Roll about the thrust axis is the hardest to see.
A gyro measures *rates*. Integrating rates gives attitude *changes*, not the absolute attitude.

interactive.instructions: Run the observability check in different configurations: one station vs several, range-only vs range+bearing, star tracker on/off, before vs during the thrust arc. Switch experiments with the variant selector.
steps: Check rank with a 0 s window (a single epoch).
Switch to the attitude variant and check rank before and during the thrust arc.

hints.text: A single range is one number — rank 1. A pass of ranges gives more, but poorly conditioned.

reasoning.prompt: The observability matrix has full rank over a 5-minute pass of range-only data. Does that guarantee an accurate orbit?

options.text: Yes — full rank means everything is determined.
options.feedback: Full rank means every direction has *some* information. It can still be very little (huge condition number).

options.text: No — it's a local, linearised test; a large condition number means some directions are only weakly determined.
options.feedback: Exactly. Rank answers 'can I see it at all?'; the condition number and the best-case σ answer 'how well?'.

debrief.markdown:
**Geometry decides what you can know.** Range-only tracking measures one number; bearing adds two more; consecutive samples add velocity through the dynamics. Attitude hides from position sensors until a thrust arc couples it into the orbit.

*Placeholder for your notes:* extend with a GNSS + one-station comparison or a star-tracker outage experiment.
